extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, in-house counsel, and applicants seeking patent and trademark protection in Argentina and Brazil
extracted.subtask_description: Country-specific prosecution and litigation standards for patents and trademarks in Argentina and Brazil, including substantive patentability criteria, application formalities, oppositions, enforcement remedies, procedural timelines, and claim-drafting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness and confusing similarity (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks must not be visually, phonetically and ideologically similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider type of consumer for the goods/services, whether the trademarks are famous, prior coexistence in the market, inclusion of common ingredients, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark application formalities (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: File an application for each individual class including applicant’s name, address, description of the trademark, indication of products/services, priority country and serial number (priority certificate within 90 days), and Power of Attorney (signature notarized and legalized with Apostille — should be filed within 40 days from application filing in AR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: *Items marked with an asterisk are requested to obtain a filing date. Remaining items can be filed later (note applies across jurisdictions on filing formalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant opposition period (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may file opposition to a trademark application within 30 days following the Argentine publication of the trademark application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After grant, third parties can still file a nullity action with Argentine Federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution delay expectation (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average prosecution term approximately 14 to 18 months from application date; longer if opposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection provided by pending trademark applications (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark rights are enforceable in Argentina only once the trademark has been granted; no enforceability between filing date and granting date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During pendency send out-of-court notice to an infringer; the only right derived from an application is the priority right to file in a third country and claim priority from the AR prior application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews allowed (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner interviews are allowed and are helpful to overcome office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name registration criteria (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain names registered with NIC Argentina on a first-come, first-serve basis; there is a procedure to challenge registrations that conflict with trademark rights or where another party holds a better right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration via AR Registrar webpage after paying official fee; term is one year, renewable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark infringement definition (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use in the market of a trademark identical or similar to one already registered to distinguish the same or similar products/services constitutes trademark infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions usually filed in Argentine Civil and Commercial Federal courts; per article 31 of trademark law infringement can also be prosecuted as a crime before criminal courts; no administrative actions available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to sue for trademark infringement (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark owner is entitled to bring suit; a contractual licensee may have the right to exercise legal actions of the owner if properly authorized in the contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges’ IP expertise (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil and Commercial Federal courts are competent to decide trademark infringement; judges are experienced and have knowledge of IP law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation timeframes (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: First instance trademark infringement actions can take 2–4 years; Court of Appeals procedures 1–2 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation venue restriction (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: No administrative courts for patents and trademarks; litigation filed and decided by Judges of the Federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for trademark damages (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: If compensation of damages is claimed, there is a term of three (3) years to bring the case since the infringement or one (1) year from the day the owner had knowledge of the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions and interim relief (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may request preliminary injunctions: embargo of objects, inventory/description, seizure of objects, injunction to prevent entry into market, preservation of evidence (art. 50 of TRIPS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies are ex-parte procedures; defendant can intervene after remedy is executed. Bonds are requested to grant temporary injunction or other remedies; remedies executed once owner deposits bond determined by court. Preliminary injunctions can be appealed/revoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in trademark cases (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden of proof of infringement lies on the trademark owner alleging infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert evidence is not common; trademark cases are not usually decided considering witnesses evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney fees and pre-decision payment requirement (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before issuing a final decision, judge will demand plaintiff to pay a tax equivalent to 3% of the amount requested as compensation for damages; losing party will pay attorney’s fees set by judge between 11% to 20% of amount of damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punitive damages are not provided in Argentine legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and pre-trial procedures (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: No discovery in Argentina; pre-trial preliminary measures aimed at preserving evidence or obtaining documents may be requested to the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediation is a mandatory pretrial procedure before filing a lawsuit; not required for requesting a temporary injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability in trademark enforcement (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: No personal liability for corporations on trademark infringements; individuals may have to pay plaintiff’s attorneys’ fees if found responsible; criminal procedures can impose personal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee shifting in trademark litigation (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Losing party obliged to support attorney fees determined by judge (11%-20% of amounts discussed); if no money involved judge fixes fees based on complexity and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal timing and procedure (Argentina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to Federal Civil and Commercial Appeals courts: five working days to file appeal once decision notified; then five working days to ground the appeal after Appeals court receives record. For constitutional issues, Supreme Court appeal term is ten working days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure is written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and ADR in Argentina (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation proceedings are mandatory before filing a lawsuit; arbitration is rarely used for IP matters; cases can be settled at any instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable an invention must meet novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazilian IP Statute lists non-eligible subject matter (discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, abstract concepts, business methods, software per se, methods of treatment/diagnosis, natural living beings and biological materials found in nature or isolated, natural biological processes, and anything contrary to morals or public safety/health/order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs and utility models (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs are ornamental forms or arrangements (new and original visual configuration) and may be protected; utility model is an object of practical use with new shape/arrangement and an inventive act resulting in functional improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design applications are granted without substantive examination; utility models treated separately with defined term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical patent pre-approval (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting of patents for pharmaceutical products/processes depends on prior approval from ANVISA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a linkage-like requirement though no US-style Orange Book exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claims and written description scrutiny (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Markush claims are allowed but subject to scrutiny whether the application complies with written description/enablement and whether claims are fully supported by the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material deposits (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: If biological material is essential and cannot be properly described or is not accessible to the public, the specification must be supplemented by a deposit in an institution authorized by the Brazilian PTO or indicated in an international agreement such as the Budapest Treaty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and software-implemented inventions (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Software per se (lines of code) is not patentable and is protected via registration (copyright-like); software-implemented inventions that protect an invention are patentable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and inventive step determination (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: New when not included in the state of the art; inventive step exists when invention is not evident/obvious to a person skilled in the art. State of the art comprises everything accessible to the public before filing date by any means, in Brazil or abroad, subject to grace period and priority provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of novelty the whole contents of an application filed in Brazil but not yet published may be considered state of the art from filing/priority date if published later. Grace period: disclosure by inventor or certain specified sources within 12 months preceding filing/priority is not part of the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim clarity and drafting requirements (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be based on the specification, characterize particularities, and define clearly and precisely the subject matter to be protected. Each claim must define technical characteristics in a clear, precise and positive manner, avoiding expressions that result in lack of definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazilian PTO guidelines: (i) claims should begin with the title or part of the title corresponding to its category, containing 'characterized by' only once; (ii) define characteristics clearly and positively; (iii) be fully grounded in the specification; (iv) avoid references to specification/drawings (e.g., 'as set forth in the specification'); (v) when drawings used, include reference indicators in brackets if necessary (but indicators impose no constraints on claims); (vi) no bullet point interruptions; (vii) have no segments explaining functioning, advantages or simple use of the object, as these will not be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable methods and allowable second medical use claims (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain methods (business methods, mathematical methods, natural biological processes) and methods of treatment/diagnosis are not patentable subject matter; second medical use and Swiss-type claims are allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME fee reductions and expedited examination pilots (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees up to 60% lower for natural persons, local small companies, research institutions, NGOs, and government entities; pilot programs allow small companies to request expedited examination and other pilot programs (PPH with USPTO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application formalities and required items (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application must include title, one or more claims, petition with applicant/inventor details, specification, abstract, drawings if necessary, power of attorney, payment of fees, certified copy of priority application, genetic resource access number if applicable, and number of biological deposit certificate if applicable (this information must be included in the specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties may file documents/arguments to assist examination until end of examination; post-grant opposition available within six months from grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection by pending patent applications (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: No protection provided by pending applications; enforcement of patent rights occurs after grant. Possible to request damages for acts of infringement occurred after date of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim amendments allowed up to request for examination limited to subject matter originally disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and lack of extensions (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent term for invention is 20 years from filing (or 10 years from grant if beneficial to owner); utility models 15 years from filing (or 7 years from grant). Patent term extensions are not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important in light of backlog at Brazilian PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional practice (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application may, until the end of examination, be divided into two or more applications provided divisional references original and does not exceed disclosed matter; divisional retains filing date and priority benefit of original; fees apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited examination eligibility (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expedited examination available for technologies related to certain diseases, green technologies, elderly or persons with certain conditions, national emergency or public interest, pilot programs for small companies and applications originally filed in Brazil, and PPH pilot with USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previsional applications not available (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional applications are not available in Brazil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent infringement scope and exceptions (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner may prevent third parties from manufacturing, using, offering for sale, selling or importing a patented product, process, or product directly obtained by a patented process; defendant may be required to prove a different manufacturing process for process patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts not considered infringement include private non-commercial acts, experimental use for research, preparation of medicine per prescription for individual cases, products placed on internal market by patentee (exhaustion), certain uses of patented living matter without economic interest, and acts to obtain regulatory approval (Bolar-type use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent infringement procedural stages (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical stages: preparation and filing of complaint and request for preliminary ex parte injunctive relief; decision on injunction (interlocutory appeal possible); service/mandatory settlement hearing; defendant response; plaintiff reply; expert examination; closing arguments; decision on merits; appeal stages thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing and declaratory actions (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner and, under certain circumstances, the licensee has standing to file infringement action; declaratory judgment actions of non-infringement are available and can be used as strategy or forum-shopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges’ IP expertise and need to educate (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states have business courts specialized in IP with experience; other courts rarely deal with patent cases and judges often lack expertise, so litigants should educate the judge through in-chambers meetings and briefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary ex parte injunctive relief requirements (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary ex parte injunctions are widely available and sometimes can be obtained in less than 24 hours; to obtain such relief plaintiff must show likelihood of prevailing on merits and irreparable harm if not granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctive relief often consists of search and seizure orders and orders to immediately cease infringement. Posting a bond is not required but judge may request one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcated invalidity system (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity actions are decided by federal district courts and the Brazilian PTO is a mandatory co-defendant; infringement issues are decided by state trial courts; current case law holds invalidity cannot be raised as defense in infringement actions and must be decided in a separate lawsuit filed in federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence, expert testimony and burden of proof (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties can produce witness testimony, expert opinions, documents, depositions, site inspections. Expert evidence is extremely important; courts will often request a court-appointed expert to answer technical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically burden of proof lies on the plaintiff; for methods/process patents the defendant has burden to prove product was obtained by a different process; in invalidity lawsuits, if PTO argues patent invalid, defendant may de facto bear burden to establish patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages calculation methods (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages can be calculated based on lost profits, profits made by the defendant, or reasonable royalties — whichever is more favorable to the plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and appellate practice (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Losing party has right to appeal before appellate court (de novo review); further appeals to Superior Court of Justice if federal statutes violated and to Supreme Court if constitutional issues; interlocutory decisions (e.g., injunction grants/rejections) can be challenged by interlocutory appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement, ADR and PTO consent for invalidity settlement (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may voluntarily settle infringement cases; invalidity lawsuits can only be settled if Brazilian PTO (mandatory co-defendant) agrees; mediation and arbitration available but rarely used in infringement and invalidity actions; settlement hearing often a pre-trial mandatory proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee shifting and attorney fees (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Losing party is normally ordered to pay a certain amount as attorney fees, but amounts set by Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and judge are typically a very small fraction of actual attorneys’ fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability for patent infringement (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: No personal liability except in criminal cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust risk when enforcing patents (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sham litigation complaints may be filed before Antitrust Authorities; patent owners should frame cases to minimize antitrust risk; Antitrust Authorities have fined companies for alleged sham litigation and antitrust complaints have been used against standard-essential patent enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of trademarks registrable (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominative, figurative, combined and three-dimensional signs can be registered as trademarks; any visually perceptive distinctive sign not prohibited may be registered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audible, olfactory and taste signs cannot be registered since statute only provides protection of visually perceptive signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark distinctiveness analysis (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks must be sufficiently distinct compared to other signs; criteria for analyzing distinctiveness are comparison of ideological, phonetic and visual elements considering the specific class and prior coexistence in the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark application formalities (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications require electronic request with applicant information, information about the mark and international classification(s), power of attorney, proof of payment of official fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical registration without oppositions/rejections takes ~2–3 years; if pre-grant oppositions or initial rejection, final decision usually 4–6 years. Provisional applications are not allowed.
